1.title: Cost-Optimized Databases
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Cost-Optimized Databases. This module covers task statement four point three, the third task of Domain four, Design Cost-Optimized Architectures. You will choose the cheapest database type and engine, plan capacity, use caches and proxies to avoid bigger databases, control backup cost, pick columnar and time series stores, and plan migrations. The exam describes a data model and a traffic shape, and asks for the cheapest fit.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Choose the cheapest database type and engine for a workload. Plan capacity: instance size, capacity units and serverless options. Use caching, read replicas and connection proxies to avoid bigger databases. Set backup and retention policies that control storage cost. And pick columnar and time series stores, and plan migrations between engines.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Trims the Database Bill
1.text: The database bill at Lantern and Loom keeps growing. The orders table has unpredictable traffic. The Aurora cluster is heavy on I O and costs more every month. Lambda functions open too many connections. Sensor readings from the warehouse pile up. And snapshots from years ago are still billing. Your job is to cut the bill and keep recovery.

1.title: Choosing a Cost-Effective Database
1.text: Start with the need. Key-value at any scale, paying per use, means DynamoDB. Relational, with joins and transactions, means R D S or Aurora. Analytics over huge tables means Redshift, which is columnar. Time series, such as sensors, means Timestream. Cassandra-compatible wide column means Keyspaces. Hot reads call for ElastiCache or Dax in front. Open-source engines, such as My S Q L and Postgres, avoid commercial license fees. And relational is not always cheaper, so do not force non-relational data into it. Exam tip: pick the engine that fits the access pattern, then the cheapest way to run it.

1.title: Capacity Planning
1.text: Each database has its own sizing dimension. For R D S, you pay for the instance class, the storage, and Multi-A Z, and storage autoscaling can grow it. Aurora has instances plus storage that grows automatically, and replicas. Aurora Serverless version two uses Aurora capacity units that scale with load. DynamoDB uses read and write capacity units, or pay per request. Redshift uses a node type and count, or serverless capacity. Measure first, then size, because over-provisioning is the commonest waste. Compute Optimizer reviews R D S, Aurora and DynamoDB utilization. Exam tip: unknown or spiky load points to serverless or on-demand; steady load points to provisioned plus a commitment.

1.title: DynamoDB Capacity Modes and Table Classes
1.text: DynamoDB has two capacity modes, plus ways to lower the price. On-demand bills per request, so it suits unpredictable or new traffic with no planning. Provisioned bills for the capacity you set, per hour, so it suits steady, forecastable traffic. Provisioned with auto scaling follows a target utilization, for daily curves you can bound. Reserved capacity is a one or three year commitment on provisioned capacity, for a steady baseline. The Standard-I A table class has lower storage cost and higher request cost, so use it when storage is the main cost. Switching between the two capacity modes is allowed, with limits. Exam tip: spiky or unknown traffic means on-demand; steady and predictable means provisioned.

1.title: Aurora Cost Options
1.text: Aurora has several cost options. Aurora Standard bills instances, storage and a charge per I O, so it suits low to moderate I O. Aurora I O-Optimized has no I O charges, with higher instance and storage prices, so it pays off when I O is above about twenty-five percent of Aurora spend. Serverless version two bills capacity units per second and scales up and down, for variable or spiky load. Provisioned instances bill per instance hour, for steady load, with Reserved Instances. I O-Optimized applies to the whole cluster, and you can switch once every thirty days. Serverless version two can scale to zero and pause when idle. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, check the minimum capacity setting. Exam tip: when I O charges are a large share of the Aurora bill, choose I O-Optimized.

1.title: Database Savings Plans and Reserved Instances
1.text: Three commitments lower steady database cost. Database Savings Plans commit a dollar amount per hour for one year, cover Aurora, R D S, DynamoDB, ElastiCache and other database services, and save up to thirty-five percent, with lower savings on provisioned capacity. Reserved Instances cover R D S, Aurora, ElastiCache and Redshift nodes, for a specific engine and class. DynamoDB reserved capacity covers provisioned capacity, for a steady baseline only. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, Database Savings Plans follow you across engines, sizes and Regions. A workload gets one discount, because plans and Reserved Instances do not stack. Exam tip: a steady database baseline means commit, but check current coverage and discounts before you rely on them.

1.title: Caching, Read Replicas and Connection Pooling
1.text: Four tools help you avoid a bigger database. ElastiCache serves hot reads from memory, so the database can be smaller. DynamoDB Accelerator, called Dax, is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB reads, at microsecond latency. Read replicas offload reads, and cost less than a larger primary when reads dominate. R D S Proxy pools connections, so Lambda or bursty applications need smaller instances. With cache-aside, you check the cache, then the database, then fill the cache. Replicas add instance and storage cost, so add them only for read pressure. Exam tip: read-heavy, repeated queries mean cache first; many short connections mean R D S Proxy.

1.title: Backup and Retention Policies
1.text: Backup cost is controlled by retention and by copies. The figure shows a timeline: an automated backup window that ends at the retention period, a point-in-time recovery marker inside it, manual snapshots that stay until deleted, and an archive step at the far right. R D S automated backups keep from zero to thirty-five days, and free backup storage equals one hundred percent of your provisioned storage in a Region. Manual snapshots stay until deleted, so delete the ones you do not need. Snapshots are incremental, and cross-Region copies add storage and transfer cost. DynamoDB offers point-in-time recovery up to thirty-five days, plus on-demand backups. A W S Backup lifecycle moves copies to cold storage and expires them. Exam tip: use the shortest retention that meets the recovery goal, and delete manual snapshots you no longer need.

2.title: Columnar and Time Series Stores
2.text: Specialized stores can cut cost for the right data. Amazon Redshift is a columnar warehouse. R A three nodes separate compute from storage, you can pause and resume, serverless suits light use, and Reserved Instances suit steady use. Amazon Timestream holds time series data in memory and magnetic tiers with retention, and needs no servers. Amazon Keyspaces is wide column, Cassandra-compatible, with on-demand or provisioned capacity. S three with Athena queries data in place and charges per query, which is best for ad hoc analysis. Pausing stops compute billing, but storage still bills. Exam tip: occasional analytics means serverless or Athena; a steady twenty-four hour warehouse means provisioned with reserved nodes.

2.title: Choosing Engines and Migrating
2.text: Migration tools depend on the engines. A homogeneous migration keeps the same engine. The Database Migration Service, D M S, often does a lift and shift, with continuous replication possible. A heterogeneous migration changes engine, so use D M S Schema Conversion first for the schema and code, then D M S to move the data. Moving from a commercial engine to Aurora or open-source R D S removes license fees. D M S bills for the replication instance, or serverless, by the hour, so stop it when you are done. Choose the engine for features and skills first, then license and run cost. Between My S Q L and Postgres, pick by application support, not price. Exam tip: a cheaper database through a different engine means a heterogeneous migration with schema conversion and D M S.

2.title: Stop Idle and Non-Production Databases
2.text: Idle databases still cost money unless you act. Stopping an R D S or Aurora instance removes the instance charge, though storage still bills, and it restarts automatically after seven days. Single-A Z for development and test avoids the second instance. Serverless version two for development scales down when idle. Smaller classes off hours use fewer capacity units or node hours. Delete unused snapshots and idle replicas to remove ongoing storage and instance cost. Keep Multi-A Z and replicas for production only, and use cost allocation tags on databases. Cost Explorer, Budgets and the Cost and Usage Report show the spend, and consolidated billing shares discounts. Exam tip: for test databases that are idle at night, stop them or use serverless, not Multi-A Z.

2.title: Choosing the Cheapest Database
2.text: Here is the chooser. The figure branches from the workload to the database service and capacity mode. Key-value with unknown traffic means DynamoDB on-demand. Key-value with steady traffic means DynamoDB provisioned with auto scaling. Relational and variable means Aurora Serverless version two. Relational and steady means R D S or Aurora with a commitment. Analytics means Redshift or Athena, and sensors mean Timestream. Exam tip: name the data model and the traffic shape, then pick the cheapest capacity model.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Cost-Optimized Databases
2.text: Here is what the exam asks. Which database type fits the data and the cost. Which capacity mode: on-demand, provisioned or serverless. Which commitment: Database Savings Plans, Reserved Instances or reserved capacity. Which backup and retention policy controls storage cost. And which migration tool moves data between engines. Exam tip: look for the clues: unpredictable, steady, I O heavy, sensors, idle and license.

2.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Trims the Database Bill
2.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Unpredictable orders traffic: DynamoDB on-demand. An I O-heavy Aurora cluster: Aurora I O-Optimized. Lambda connection storms: R D S Proxy. Sensor readings: Timestream with retention. Old snapshots still billing: delete them, and shorten retention. A steady relational baseline: a Database Savings Plan or Reserved Instances. And idle test databases: stop them, or use serverless.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Pick the type by access pattern: DynamoDB, R D S, Aurora, Redshift or Timestream. Pick the capacity model: on-demand or serverless for spiky load, provisioned plus a commitment for steady load. Avoid bigger databases with a cache, read replicas and R D S Proxy. Control copies with the shortest retention, and delete manual snapshots. And migrate with D M S, adding schema conversion for a new engine.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. The Lantern and Loom orders table has unpredictable traffic, with long quiet periods and sudden bursts. The team does not want to plan capacity or pay for unused throughput. Which option fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode. It bills per request with no capacity planning, which suits unpredictable traffic.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A steady Aurora cluster at Lantern and Loom pays a large per-I O charge that is more than twenty-five percent of its Aurora bill. The workload is stable. What should the architect do to cut cost? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: switch the cluster to Aurora I O-Optimized. It removes per-I O charges, in exchange for higher instance and storage prices, and pays off when I O is a large share of spend.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two actions reduce database backup cost while still meeting the recovery goal? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Set automated backup retention to the shortest period that meets the recovery goal, and delete manual snapshots that are no longer needed. Extra Region copies, maximum retention and keeping every snapshot all add cost.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Warehouse sensors send readings every few seconds, and queries ask for trends over time windows. The team wants a serverless store built for this data, with older data moved to cheaper storage. Which service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Amazon Timestream. It is a serverless time series database with memory and magnetic tiers and retention settings.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Hundreds of Lambda functions open database connections at Lantern and Loom, which forces the team to run a much larger R D S instance than the queries need. How can they reduce cost? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: place R D S Proxy in front of the database. It pools and shares connections, so the database can be smaller.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: C and E. Question four: D. Question five: C. In Module fourteen, we cut the cost of network architectures.
